newsitem.title: USA: Jurors see mangled axle of truck in Okla. blast.
newsitem.headline: Jurors see mangled axle of truck in Okla. blast.

text.p: A twisted rear axle from the truck used in the deadly Oklahoma City blast was shown to bombing trial jurors on Tuesday by prosecutors who said the mangled metal tied the explosion to defendant Timothy McVeigh.

An identification number from the axle led authorities to a Junction City, Kansas, rental agency, where prosecutors say McVeigh rented the Ryder truck that carried the bomb that blew up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people.

Prosecutors focused on physical evidence against McVeigh, who has pleaded not guilty to murder and conspiracy. They have said his fingerprints were found on a receipt for the truck rental and traces of explosives were found on his clothing.
The mangled 250-pound (115-kg) truck axle was propelled almost 200 yards (metres) in the air from the force of the April 19, 1995, blast and crashed onto a parked car, prosecutors said.

Also part of the prosecution's presentation of physical evidence was an FBI agent who testified that he found McVeigh's fingerprint on a handwritten note that read "TNT at $5 a stick. Need more. Call after 01 May, see if I can get some more."

The note, written on the back of a crumpled business card for a Wisconsin military supply store, was discovered in the car of the Oklahoma state trooper who arrested McVeigh for driving without a licence plate less than two hours after the blast. The trooper said he found the card behind the front seat where the handcuffed McVeigh rode to the local jail.

As he has since the trial began last week, McVeigh appeared to listen closely. Wearing a light blue shirt and white pants, his dark hair trimmed in a crewcut, he leaned his head on his chin as he sat at the defence table, at times taking notes.
The FBI agent, Louis Hupp, told the jury McVeigh was cooperative when he took his fingerprints after his arrest.
Authorities said they connected McVeigh to the bombing later through the axle of the truck, which they said he rented in Junction City under the assumed name Robert Kling.
McVeigh was identified by a Junction City motel owner who has said he registered there under his own name. The motel owner has not testified in the trial.
Prosecutors also had a model of the Oklahoma City blast scene for jurors to see. An FBI agent testified that damage from the bomb spread about 16 blocks in the city's downtown.
McVeigh faces the death penalty if convicted.
